Session 9 — Vision Transformers¶

Sebastián Ríos Saucedo · Computer Vision & Speech Recognition · EADA

Question: a Transformer was made to translate sentences. How does it look at an image, and how does it compare with a CNN?

The plan (class notebook, adapted to my repo and my Milestone 1 split)

  1. Cut a lesion into patches: the image becomes a list of tokens. → ✏️ Exercise 1
  2. Attention from scratch, checked on slide 12's numbers. → ✏️ Exercise 2
  3. Inside a pretrained ViT-B/16: follow one image, shape by shape. → ✏️ Exercise 3
  4. A ViT next to a CNN, fairly (same split, same frozen setup, same head, same metric). → ✏️ Exercise 4
  5. Milestone 4: the comparison table, a paired bootstrap, my Session 7 CNNs as reference, and the test set once.

How to run: VS Code → venv kernel → Restart → Run All. Tables / JSON go to outputs/session_09/, figures to figures/session9_*.png. Images and features are cached in ~/.cache/milk10k (outside git and OneDrive).

0.3 prep: scale the pixels like ImageNet¶

Both backbones today were pretrained on ImageNet, so the input is scaled the same way (Session 7).

In [3]:
MEAN = torch.tensor([0.485, 0.456, 0.406], device=device).view(1, 3, 1, 1)
STD = torch.tensor([0.229, 0.224, 0.225], device=device).view(1, 3, 1, 1)

def prep(xb):
    """uint8 (n, 3, 224, 224) -> float, ImageNet-normalized, on the device."""
    return (xb.to(device).float() / 255 - MEAN) / STD

1. From an image to a list of patches · slide 14¶

A ViT cuts the 224×224 image into 16×16 squares: 224 / 16 = 14 per side → 196 patches. Each patch is flattened into 16 × 16 × 3 = 768 numbers: one token.

✏️ Exercise 1 — patchify¶

Two loops (rows, then columns, every 16 pixels); take img[r:r+p, c:c+p] (16×16×3), flatten it with .reshape(-1), and stack all of them. The order is row by row, top-left to bottom-right.

In [4]:
lesion = X_val[0].permute(1, 2, 0).numpy()      # one lesion as (224, 224, 3)

def patchify(img, p=16):
    """Cut img (H, W, 3) into p x p patches; return one flattened patch per row."""
    patches = []
    for r in range(0, img.shape[0], p):          # rows: 0, 16, 32, ...
        for c in range(0, img.shape[1], p):      # columns, left to right
            patches.append(img[r:r+p, c:c+p].reshape(-1))   # 16x16x3 -> 768 numbers
    return np.array(patches)

check("patch 14 = first square of the 2nd row", ok and np.array_equal(patches[14], lesion[16:32, 0:16].reshape(-1)))

2. Attention from scratch · slides 11–12¶

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d) · V — compare, scale, softmax, mix.

✏️ Exercise 2 — attention¶

Q, K, V have one row per token and d columns. Returns the output (each row = weighted average of the rows of V) and the weights (each row adds up to 1).

In [7]:
def attention(Q, K, V):
    """Scaled dot-product attention. Returns (output, weights)."""
    d = Q.shape[1]
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)                                           # 1-2. compare + scale
    weights = np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)   # 3. softmax per row
    output = weights @ V                                                    # 4. mix
    return output, weights
In [8]:
# CHECK Exercise 2 — slide 12: Q = K = V = X
X = np.array([[1., 0.],      # token A
              [0., 1.],      # token B
              [1., 1.]])     # token C
out, w = attention(X, X, X)
ok = w is not None
check("each row of weights adds up to 1", ok and np.allclose(w.sum(axis=1), 1))
check("row C of weights = [0.248, 0.248, 0.503]", ok and np.allclose(w[2], [0.248, 0.248, 0.503], atol=1e-3))
check("output of C = [0.752, 0.752]", ok and np.allclose(out[2], [0.752, 0.752], atol=1e-3))

# the same formula as PyTorch's built-in version, on 196 random tokens
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Q, K, V = (rng.normal(size=(196, 64)) for _ in range(3))
torch_out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(*(torch.tensor(a) for a in (Q, K, V))).numpy()
check("same as PyTorch on 196 tokens", ok and np.allclose(attention(Q, K, V)[0], torch_out))

2.1 Attention does not know the order · slide 16¶

Shuffle the tokens → the outputs come out shuffled the same way, with the same values. That's why a ViT adds a position embedding.

In [9]:
perm = rng.permutation(196)
out_original, _ = attention(Q, K, V)
out_shuffled, _ = attention(Q[perm], K[perm], V[perm])
print("same values, just in another order:", np.allclose(out_shuffled, out_original[perm]))   # True

same values, just in another order: True

✏️ Exercise 3 — follow one image through the ViT¶

  1. Patch embedding output (1, 768, 14, 14) → list of 196 tokens: flatten(2) joins 14×14 into 196, transpose(1, 2) puts tokens before channels → (1, 196, 768).
  2. Put the class token in front → (1, 197, 768). (expand copies it once per image of the batch.)
  3. vit.encoder adds the position embedding and runs the 12 blocks; only the class token (position 0) goes to the head → (1, 1000).
In [11]:
x = prep(X_val[:1])                          # one lesion: (1, 3, 224, 224)
with torch.no_grad():
    h = vit.conv_proj(x)                     # patch embedding: (1, 768, 14, 14)
    h = h.flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)         # (1) list of tokens   -> (1, 196, 768)
    h = torch.cat([vit.class_token.expand(h.shape[0], -1, -1), h], dim=1)   # (2) add class token -> (1, 197, 768)
    z = vit.encoder(h)                       # + position, 12 blocks -> (1, 197, 768)
    logits = vit.heads(z[:, 0])              # (3) class token -> head -> (1, 1000)
In [12]:
# CHECK Exercise 3
check(f"tokens + class token: (1, 197, 768) -> got {tuple(h.shape)}", tuple(h.shape) == (1, 197, 768))
check(f"output of the head: (1, 1000) -> got {tuple(logits.shape)}", tuple(logits.shape) == (1, 1000))
with torch.no_grad():
    check("your steps give exactly vit(x)", torch.allclose(logits, vit(x), atol=1e-4))

3.1 A real attention map · slide 21¶

Where does the class token look in the last block? torchvision computes these weights but doesn't return them, so this cell asks for them for a moment. Bright = more attention. Not a medical explanation: this ViT learned on everyday photos. I show one lesion of each class from my validation set.

In [13]:
def cls_attention(images):
    layer = vit.encoder.layers[-1].self_attention
    original_forward, saved = layer.forward, {}
    def forward_with_weights(q, k, v, **kwargs):
        kwargs["need_weights"] = True                    # ask for the weights (torchvision says False)
        out, weights = original_forward(q, k, v, **kwargs)
        saved["w"] = weights                             # (batch, 197, 197), averaged over the 12 heads
        return out, weights
    layer.forward = forward_with_weights
    try:
        with torch.no_grad():
            vit(prep(images))
    finally:
        layer.forward = original_forward                 # always back to normal
    return saved["w"][:, 0, 1:].reshape(-1, 14, 14).cpu()   # class-token row, without itself

idx = [int((y_val == c).nonzero()[0]) for c in range(3)] + [int((y_val == 2).nonzero()[1])]   # one per class + 1
att = cls_attention(X_val[idx])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(13, 6.5))
for j, i in enumerate(idx):
    big = F.interpolate(att[j][None, None], size=224, mode="bilinear")[0, 0]     # 14x14 -> 224x224
    axes[0, j].imshow(X_val[i].permute(1, 2, 0)); axes[0, j].set_title(CLASSES[y_val[i]])
    axes[1, j].imshow(X_val[i].permute(1, 2, 0)); axes[1, j].imshow(big, cmap="inferno", alpha=0.6)
for ax in axes.ravel():
    ax.axis("off")

4. A ViT next to a CNN, fairly · slides 23, 25¶

Same lesions, same frozen setup, same head, same training, same metric: only the backbone changes. Each lesion becomes one vector once (ResNet-18: 512 numbers after global average pooling; ViT: 768 numbers, the class token), then only a new last layer is trained.

4.1 Compute the features once (the slow step)¶

Adapted: I also embed my test set now (it's the same cost and it lets Section 5 open it once at the end without re-running the backbone). Features are cached in ~/.cache/milk10k, so next session (11 classes) they load in a second.

In [14]:
from torchvision.models import resnet18, ResNet18_Weights

def backbone(name):
    if name == "resnet18":
        net = resnet18(weights=ResNet18_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1)
        net.fc = nn.Identity()                    # output: 512 numbers instead of 1000 classes
    else:
        net = vit_b_16(weights=ViT_B_16_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1)
        net.heads = nn.Identity()                 # output: the class token, 768 numbers
    return net.to(device).eval()

EMBED_S = {}
def features(name, X, split):
    f = CACHE_DIR / f"s9_features_{name}_{split}_{len(X)}_seed{config.SEED}.pt"
    if not f.exists():
        net, t0 = backbone(name), time.perf_counter()
        with torch.no_grad():
            out = torch.cat([net(prep(X[i:i + 64])).cpu() for i in range(0, len(X), 64)])   # 64 images at a time
        torch.save(out, f)
        EMBED_S[f"{name}_{split}"] = round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1)
        print(f"{name} {split}: {tuple(out.shape)} in {EMBED_S[f'{name}_{split}']:.0f} s")
    return torch.load(f, weights_only=True)

BACKBONES = ["resnet18", "vit_b_16"]
feats = {name: {"train": features(name, X_train, "train"),
                "val": features(name, X_val, "val"),
                "test": features(name, X_test, "test")} for name in BACKBONES}
print({name: tuple(f["train"].shape) for name, f in feats.items()})   # resnet18 (n, 512), vit_b_16 (n, 768)

✏️ Exercise 4 — the same head for both¶

train_head: one nn.Linear, class weights, Adam, 25 epochs (same recipe as Session 7). The 4 lines of a training step: forget old gradients → loss → backpropagation → update. macro_f1: class with the highest score (argmax(1)), then macro-F1.

In [15]:
def train_head(F_train, y, n_classes=3, epochs=25):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    head = nn.Linear(F_train.shape[1], n_classes)                      # the only weights we train
    class_weights = len(y) / (n_classes * torch.bincount(y, minlength=n_classes).float())
    loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=class_weights)                # rare classes count more (Session 6)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(head.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        order = torch.randperm(len(y))                                 # new random order in each epoch
        for i in range(0, len(y), 64):
            idx = order[i:i + 64]                                      # one batch of 64 lesions
            optimizer.zero_grad()                                      # 1. forget the old gradients
            loss = loss_fn(head(F_train[idx]), y[idx])                 # 2. compute the loss
            loss.backward()                                            # 3. backpropagation
            optimizer.step()                                           # 4. update the weights
    return head

def predict_head(head, F_):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return head(F_).argmax(1)                                      # class with the highest score

def macro_f1(head, F_, y):
    return float(f1_score(y, predict_head(head, F_), average="macro"))  # macro-F1 of y vs pred

5. Milestone 4 — my comparison¶

5.1 Is the difference real? Paired bootstrap on validation¶

Same tool as my Session 7 mini challenge: resample the 749 validation lesions 2,000 times, recompute both macro-F1s on the same resample, look at the 95% interval of the difference (ViT − ResNet). If it contains 0, the gap could be noise.

In [ ]:
def paired_bootstrap(y, pred_a, pred_b, n=2000, seed=0):
    """95% CI of macro-F1(b) - macro-F1(a) on the same resampled lesions, and P(b > a)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    y, pred_a, pred_b = map(np.asarray, (y, pred_a, pred_b))
    diffs = np.empty(n)
    for k in range(n):
        i = rng.integers(0, len(y), len(y))
        f = lambda p: f1_score(y[i], p[i], average="macro", labels=[0, 1, 2], zero_division=0)
        diffs[k] = f(pred_b) - f(pred_a)
    return np.percentile(diffs, [2.5, 97.5]), float((diffs > 0).mean())

ci, p_vit_better = paired_bootstrap(y_val, val_pred["resnet18"], val_pred["vit_b_16"])
print(f"ViT - ResNet-18 (val macro-F1): {val_f1['vit_b_16'] - val_f1['resnet18']:+.3f}, "
      f"95% CI [{ci[0]:+.3f}, {ci[1]:+.3f}], P(ViT better) = {p_vit_better:.2f}")

The two frozen rows are the fair comparison (same everything except the backbone). Session 7 numbers use all 3,742 training lesions, so with FULL = False they are not directly comparable.

        "feature size": feats[name]["train"].shape[1],
        "embed train+val+test (s)": sum(EMBED_S.get(f"{name}_{s}", np.nan) for s in ("train", "val", "test")),
        "val macro-F1": round(val_f1[name], 3),
    }
rows[f"S7 - {s7[best_s7]['label']} (reference)"] = {
    "backbone weights": s7[best_s7]["total_params"], "trainable weights": s7[best_s7]["trainable_params"],
    "feature size": 512, "embed train+val+test (s)": np.nan, "val macro-F1": round(s7[best_s7]["best_val_f1"], 3)}
table = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
table.to_csv(OUT / "comparison.csv")

5.3 The test set, once¶

The winner between the two frozen backbones is chosen on validation. Only then its test macro-F1 is computed (plus a bootstrap 95% interval). Run this only with FULL = True: that is the number that goes in the Milestone 4 report.

In [ ]:
RUN_TEST = FULL                                                # open the test set only on the final run

winner = max(BACKBONES, key=lambda n: val_f1[n])               # chosen on validation, not on test
RESULTS.update({"full_train": FULL, "n_train": int(len(y_train)), "val_f1": val_f1,
                "val_delta_vit_minus_resnet": round(val_f1["vit_b_16"] - val_f1["resnet18"], 4),
                "val_delta_ci95": [round(float(c), 4) for c in ci], "p_vit_better": round(p_vit_better, 3),
                "head_train_seconds": train_s, "embed_seconds": EMBED_S, "winner_on_val": winner,
                "val_pred": {n: p.tolist() for n, p in val_pred.items()}})

if RUN_TEST:
    test_pred = predict_head(heads[winner], feats[winner]["test"]).numpy()
    yt = y_test.numpy()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    boots = [f1_score(yt[i], test_pred[i], average="macro", labels=[0, 1, 2], zero_division=0)
             for i in (rng.integers(0, len(yt), len(yt)) for _ in range(2000))]
    RESULTS["test"] = {"model": winner, "macro_f1": round(float(f1_score(yt, test_pred, average="macro")), 4),
                       "accuracy": round(float(accuracy_score(yt, test_pred)), 4),
                       "ci95": [round(float(v), 4) for v in np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])],
                       "confusion": confusion_matrix(yt, test_pred, labels=[0, 1, 2]).tolist()}
    print(RESULTS["test"])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 4.2))
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(yt, test_pred, display_labels=CLASSES, cmap="Oranges", ax=ax, colorbar=False)
    ax.set_title(f"{winner} frozen + linear head\nTEST ({len(yt)} lesions)", fontsize=9)
    fig.savefig(FIG / "session9_winner_test_confusion.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()
else:
    print(f"winner on validation: {winner}. Test set stays closed (FULL = False).")
save_results()

5.4 Conclusion (class run: FULL = False, 1,000 training lesions)¶

  • Fair comparison (both frozen + the same linear head): ViT-B/16 reaches a validation macro-F1 of 0.606 vs 0.530 for ResNet-18 (+0.076). The paired bootstrap gives a 95% CI of [+0.026, +0.127] and P(ViT better) ≈ 1.00: the interval does not contain 0, so the gap is real, not noise.
  • Why: the ViT's class token gathers information from all 196 patches in every block (global context from layer 1), while frozen ResNet-18 features come from local filters averaged at the end. The ImageNet features of the ViT transfer better to lesions without any fine-tuning.
  • Cost: the ViT has ~7.7× more backbone weights (85.8 M vs 11.2 M) and computing its features took ~13× longer on my CPU (1,116 s vs 85 s for train + val + test). Training the head itself takes under 1 s for both.
  • Against my best CNN (Session 7, ResNet-18 fully fine-tuned, val 0.676): the frozen ViT is still below it, but it uses only 2,307 trainable weights and 1,000 training lesions. The fair next step is to repeat this with FULL = True (all 3,742 lesions) and, if possible, fine-tune the ViT too.
  • Test set: still closed. It will be opened once, for the winner on validation, in the FULL = True run (Milestone 4).
